name: The Steenenkamer Maple

location.neighbourhood: Steenenkamer, on the IJssel floodplain near the Bolwerksmolen windmill, about 0.6km from Deventer's published dev_005 tree

story:
One of the thickest maples in the Netherlands has two trunks instead of one. It stands on the Bolwerksweg outside Deventer, past the Bolwerksmolen windmill, where the lane runs out onto the floodplain of the IJssel, and it divides low into a double stem carrying a crown far wider than the road it shades. The national tree foundation lists it among the ten most remarkable trees in the province of Overijssel.

It went into the ground somewhere between 1880 and 1890, which puts it at roughly 140 years, young for a tree on a list like this. Almost all of that life has been spent on ground the river takes back whenever the water comes up, which is not where you would expect to find a maple of this size. Deventer's own tree society had the crown pruned back not long ago, the sort of attention a tree gets once a town has decided to keep it.

It grows in a private garden. Its own record says it is clearly visible from the Bolwerksweg, and the roadside is where you stand: there is no way onto the land and no need for one.

Nobody has published a girth for it, so how thick it actually is remains an open question. If you go out there with a tape measure, tell us the number.
access: On private land (a garden) but the tree is described by bomenbieb itself as "goed zichtbaar vanaf de Bolwerksweg" (clearly visible from the public road). No public entry onto the property; view from the roadside only.
transport: Rural riverside lane, no station nearby; nearest is Deventer, roughly 15-20 minutes by bike or car from the city centre.

name: The Robinia of Kasteel Doorwerth

location.neighbourhood: Inner courtyard of Kasteel Doorwerth, a medieval moated castle near Arnhem, about 6.9km from Arnhem's published arn_003

story:
A black locust normally carries a feathery leaf made of a dozen small leaflets. This one carries a single blade, a rare cultivar called Unifoliola, and it is held locally to be the oldest black locust in the Netherlands.

Its date is genuinely disputed. The castle's own account and the Dutch tree register both say 1678: three robinias planted on the forecourt by Anton I van Aldenburg, count of Doorwerth, to mark the Peace of Nijmegen, two of them felled in the 1880s and this one not. The plaque at the tree tells a different story, crediting the Frenchman Pierre Robin with bringing the species over from the eastern United States and putting this one in around 1601, and a date of 1579 circulates as well. By the better sourced version it is about 350 years old. By the plaque it would be older still, and nobody has settled it.

What is not disputed is what it has come through. Kasteel Doorwerth, a moated medieval castle, was wrecked in the Second World War and rebuilt around it. The tree stayed where it was, and has had its crown taken back three times since, in 1965, 2010 and 2016, to keep the weight off an old frame.

The inner courtyard where it grows is free to walk into. Only the house itself costs money.

best_time.label: late May and June, when the white flower chains hang out of the crown

access: Free. The inner courtyard (binnenplein) of Kasteel Doorwerth is described by multiple independent sources as freely accessible without a ticket, with free parking on site; only entering the castle building itself is paid.
transport: Village of Doorwerth, near Arnhem/Renkum; no rail station, reachable by local bus and a short walk, or about 6.9km (a short drive or cycle) from central Arnhem.

name: The White Horse Chestnut of Poptaslot

location.neighbourhood: Front/side garden of Poptaslot, a 17th-century almshouse estate near Leeuwarden, about 4km from Leeuwarden's published lee_003

story:
Left to itself, this horse chestnut would surround itself with children. Its lowest branches sweep down to the grass and will root wherever they rest, throwing up a ring of new stems around the parent trunk. The gardener at Poptaslot cuts them back so the tree stays one tree.

It was planted in 1840 by L.P. Roodbaard, the landscape architect who redrew country estate after country estate across Friesland in the loose English style, as part of his design for the grounds here. Three maples nearby are his too, the same year, the same job. Poptaslot, also called Heringastate, was already a seventeenth century almshouse estate when he arrived, so the chestnut has spent its whole life as the newest thing on old ground.

The trunk is 4.75 metres round and the tree is 19 metres tall. In June 2017 the national tree foundation put it first on its list of the ten most beautiful trees in Friesland, ahead of older and larger trees. Not the oldest, not the biggest, just the one people wanted to stand under.

The garden is free, on weekdays from April to September, roughly nine to four and later in high summer, closed on Sundays. Going inside the house is a guided tour and a separate arrangement, but the tree is in the garden and the garden is the free part.

best_time.label: May, when the white candles come out all over the crown

access: Free. The Poptaslot garden is freely accessible on weekdays, April to September (roughly 09:00-16:00, 11:00-17:00 in July/August); only a guided tour of the house itself is paid/by appointment. Closed Sundays.
transport: Village of Marssum, near Leeuwarden; reachable by local bus, roughly 10-15 minutes from Leeuwarden centre by car.

name: The Annenborch Lime

location.neighbourhood: A small fenced mound (the site of the former Annenborch convent, burned down 1584) inside the Overlaet housing development, about 5.1km from Den Bosch's published dbo_004

story:
The convent burned down in 1584 and was never rebuilt. What is left of it is a low mound in a housing estate, and a lime tree standing on top of it.

The Annenborch was a house of Augustinian canonesses, founded in 1503 by a knight named Jan Bax, and the fire took it eighty years later. The tree came afterwards, planted on the mound somewhere between 1750 and 1800, which makes it roughly 250 years old and, by local reckoning, the oldest tree inside the boundaries of 's-Hertogenbosch. Local accounts have it surviving the severe storm of 1767, which would put it at the very early end of that planting range or push the range itself back; the two figures sit awkwardly together and nobody has reconciled them.

Since then it has watched the fields around it become the Overlaet district, which built itself around the mound rather than over it. It has been legally protected since the 1970s. Rosmalen knows it as the Annenborchboom and treats it as a local figure: in July 2022 residents of the Annenborch care home, named after the same vanished convent, went out in a convoy of wheelchairs to visit it.

It stands free and open. The fence is there for the roots, not to keep you off.

No girth or height has been published. If you measure it, tell us.
access: Free and public. Stands on a small mound in a residential green space in the Overlaet district, fenced only to protect its own roots and trunk, not to keep visitors out.
transport: In the Overlaet neighbourhood of Rosmalen, a district of 's-Hertogenbosch (Den Bosch); reachable by local bus, roughly 15-20 minutes from Den Bosch centre.
